'''Victor Robert Ambros''' (born December 1, 1953)<ref>{{Cite web |title=Who are Victor Ambros and Gary Ruvkun, winners of 2024 Nobel Prize in Medicine? |url=https://www.hindustantimes.com/world-news/who-are-victor-ambros-and-gary-ruvkun-2024-nobel-prize-in-medicine-winners-101728293721820.html |access-date=December 4, 2025 |website=Hindustan Times |language=en-US |archive-date=October 7, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241007203753/https://www.hindustantimes.com/world-news/who-are-victor-ambros-and-gary-ruvkun-2024-nobel-prize-in-medicine-winners-101728293721820.html |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Victor Ambros – Facts – 2024 |website=[[NobelPrize.org]] |publisher=Nobel Prize Outreach |year=2025 |access-date=4 December 2025 |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2024/ambros/facts/}}</ref> is an American [[Developmental biology|developmental biologist]], who discovered the first known [[microRNA]] (miRNA). He is a professor at the [[UMass Chan Medical School]]. He completed both his undergraduate and doctoral studies at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]]. Ambros received the [[Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine]] in 2024 for his research on microRNA.<ref name="NobelPrize">{{Cite web |title=Press release: The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2024 |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2024/press-release/ |access-date=October 7, 2024 |website=NobelPrize.org |language=en-US |archive-date=October 8, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241008022805/https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2024/press-release/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Biography ==

=== Early life and education ===
Ambros was born in [[Hanover, New Hampshire]]. His father, Longin Bohdan Ambros, was a Polish citizen born in 1923 in {{ill|Dordziszki|pl}}, then part of [[Second Polish Republic]] (now in [[Belarus]]); and attended [[Sigismund Augustus Gymnasium in Vilnius]] 1937–1939.<ref name="WUM">{{cite web |author=<!-- not stated --> |date=March 18, 2026 |title=We were visited by Prof. Victor Ambros – Nobel Prize winner with Polish roots |url=https://www.wum.edu.pl/en/we-were-visited-prof-victor-ambros-nobel-prize-winner-polish-roots |website=[[Medical University of Warsaw]] |access-date=September 17, 2026}}</ref><ref name="IPN">{{cite web |author=<!-- not stated --> |date=October 15, 2024 |title=Ojciec tegorocznego noblisty w bazie Instytutu Pamięci Narodowej straty.pl |url=https://ipn.gov.pl/pl/dla-mediow/komunikaty/207741,Ojciec-tegorocznego-noblisty-w-bazie-Instytutu-Pamieci-Narodowej-stratypl.html |trans-title=Father of this year's Nobel laureate in the Institute of National Remembrance's straty.pl database |website=[[Institute of National Remembrance]] |access-date=September 17, 2026}}</ref> As a teenager, Longin Ambros was deported to [[Nazi Germany]], where he was [[Forced labour under German rule during World War II|forced to work in a factory during World War II]].<ref name="WUM"/><ref name="IPN"/> At the end of war his father joined [[United States Army]] as an interpreter, and emigrated to the United States in 1946.<ref>{{cite journal |author=<!-- not stated --> |date=March 9, 2026 |title=Noblista prof. Victor Ambros stara się o polskie obywatelstwo! |url=https://forumakademickie.pl/noblista-prof-victor-ambros-stara-sie-o-polskie-obywatelstwo/ |trans-title=Nobel laureate Prof. Victor Ambros is applying for Polish citizenship! |journal=Forum Akademickie |location=[[Lublin]] |access-date=September 17, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Obituary for Longin B. Ambros at Windsor |url=https://www.knightfuneralhomes.com/obituaries/longin-ambros |website=Knight Funeral Home |access-date=October 7, 2024 |archive-date=October 7, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241007120135/https://www.knightfuneralhomes.com/obituary/2457074 |url-status=live}}</ref> In March 2026, Victor Ambros began applying for [[Polish nationality law|Polish citizenship]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Noblista prof. Victor Ambros stara się o polskie obywatelstwo |url=https://dzieje.pl/wiadomosci/noblista-prof-victor-ambros-stara-sie-o-polskie-obywatelstwo |access-date=2026-03-12 |website=dzieje.pl |language=pl}}</ref> which he was granted in September the same year.<ref>{{Cite web |title = Noblista został Polakiem. |access-date = 2026-09-16 |website = Zero.pl| language=pl |url = https://zero.pl/news/noblista-zostal-polakiem-premier-tusk-przekazal-mu-wiadomosc}}</ref> Victor grew up on a small dairy farm in [[Hartland, Vermont]], in a family of eight children and attended [[Woodstock Union High School]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Gitschier|first=Jane|date=March 5, 2010|title=In the Tradition of Science: An Interview with Victor Ambros|journal=PLOS Genetics|language=en|volume=6|issue=3|article-number=e1000853|doi=10.1371/journal.pgen.1000853|issn=1553-7404|pmc=2832673|pmid=20221254 |doi-access=free }}</ref> 

From the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]], Ambros received a [[Bachelor of Science]] with a major in biology in 1975 and a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] in biology in 1979.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Victor R. Ambros, Ph.D. |url=https://www.umassmed.edu/globalassets/ambros-lab/cv/ambros-cv_021919.pdf |access-date=2024-10-09 |website=UMass Chan Medical School |archive-date=December 2, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201202095239/https://umassmed.edu/globalassets/ambros-lab/cv/ambros-cv_021919.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-10-07 |title=Victor Ambros '75, PhD '79 and Gary Ruvkun share Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine |url=https://news.mit.edu/2024/victor-ambros-gary-ruvkun-share-nobel-prize-physiology-medicine-1007 |access-date=2024-10-09 |website=MIT News {{!}} Massachusetts Institute of Technology |language=en |archive-date=October 8, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241008030905/https://news.mit.edu/2024/victor-ambros-gary-ruvkun-share-nobel-prize-physiology-medicine-1007 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite thesis |url=https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/45675 |title=The protein covalently linked to the 5' end of poliovirus RNA. |institution=[[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] |last=Ambros |first=Victor Robert |id={{ProQuest|303013951}} |hdl=1721.1/45675 |degree=PhD}}</ref> His doctoral supervisor was [[David Baltimore]], a 1975 [[Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine|Nobel laureate in Physiology or Medicine]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Victor R Ambros PhD |url=https://profiles.umassmed.edu/display/129913 |access-date=2024-10-09 |website=UMass Chan Medical School |archive-date=October 8, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241008053830/https://profiles.umassmed.edu/display/129913 |url-status=live }}</ref> Ambros continued his research at MIT as the first postdoctoral fellow in the lab of future Nobel laureate [[H. Robert Horvitz]].<ref name="Dartmouth">{{cite web |author1=Office of Communications |title=Former Dartmouth Professor Wins Nobel Prize |url=https://home.dartmouth.edu/news/2024/10/former-dartmouth-professor-wins-nobel-prize |website=Dartmouth |access-date=9 October 2024 |date=7 October 2024}}</ref>

=== Career ===
Ambros became a faculty member at [[Harvard University]] in 1984.  However, Harvard denied tenure to Ambros shortly after he discovered what is now known as microRNA.<ref name="Cooney">{{cite news |last1=Cooney |first1=Elizabeth |title=UMass scientist Ambros wins Lasker Award |url=https://www.telegram.com/story/news/local/north/2008/09/14/umass-scientist-ambros-wins-lasker/52268029007/ |access-date=October 7, 2024 |work=[[Telegram & Gazette]] |date=September 14, 2008 |archive-date=October 7, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241007153003/https://www.telegram.com/story/news/local/north/2008/09/14/umass-scientist-ambros-wins-lasker/52268029007/ |url-status=live }}</ref>  About this, Baltimore later said in 2008: "They lost a potential Nobel laureate because they simply didn't see in him the potential that he had ... It's the nature of a seminal discovery that it's seminal in retrospect. You can't know ahead of time."<ref name="Cooney" />

Ambros joined the faculty of [[Dartmouth College]] in 1992.<ref name="Dartmouth" /> He joined the faculty at the [[University of Massachusetts Medical School]] in 2008, and currently holds the title of Silverman Professor of Natural Sciences in the program in Molecular Medicine, endowed by his former Dartmouth student, Howard Scott Silverman.<ref name="NobelPrize" /><ref name="Dartmouth" /><ref>{{cite news |last1=Schwan |first1=Henry |title='Long overdue': UMass Chan celebrates as researcher Victor Ambros wins Nobel Prize |url=https://eu.telegram.com/story/news/education/2024/10/07/victor-ambrose-researcher-at-umass-medical-school-wins-nobel-prize/75551962007/ |access-date=9 October 2024 |work=The Worcester Telegram & Gazette}}</ref>

[[File:Victor Ambros 2026.jpg|thumb|Ambros in 2026 at the [[Polish Academy of Sciences]] lecture]]

==Research==
In 1993, Ambros and his co-workers [[Rosalind Lee]] and [[Rhonda Feinbaum]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sedwick |first=Caitlin |date=2013-05-13 |title=Victor Ambros: The broad scope of microRNAs |journal=Journal of Cell Biology |volume=201 |issue=4 |pages=492–493 |doi=10.1083/jcb.2014pi|pmid=23671307 |pmc=3653358 }}</ref> reported in the journal ''[[Cell (journal)|Cell]]''<ref name="Cell">{{cite journal
 | doi = 10.1016/0092-8674(93)90529-Y
 | year = 1993
 | title = The C. Elegans heterochronic gene lin-4 encodes small RNAs with antisense complementarity to lin-14
 | journal = Cell
 | volume = 75
 | issue = 5
 | pages = 843–854
 | pmid = 8252621
 | last1 = Lee | first1 = R. C.
 | last2 = Feinbaum | first2 = R. L.
 | last3 = Ambros | first3 = V.
| doi-access = free
 }}</ref> that they had discovered single-stranded non-protein-coding regulatory [[RNA]] molecules in the organism [[Caenorhabditis elegans|''C. elegans'']]. Previous research, including work by Ambros and Horvitz,<ref>{{cite journal
 | doi = 10.1016/0092-8674(81)90501-8
 | year = 1981
 | title = Mutations that lead to reiterations in the cell lineages of C. Elegans
 | journal = Cell
 | volume = 24
 | issue = 1
 | pages = 59–69
 | pmid = 7237544
 | last1 = Chalfie | first1 = M.
 | last2 = Horvitz | first2 = H. R.
 | last3 = Sulston | first3 = J. E.
| s2cid = 33933388
 }}</ref><ref name="hierarchy">{{cite journal
 | doi = 10.1016/0092-8674(89)90171-2
 | year = 1989
 | title = A hierarchy of regulatory genes controls a larva-to-adult developmental switch in C. Elegans
 | journal = Cell
 | volume = 57
 | issue = 1
 | pages = 49–57
 | pmid = 2702689
 | last1 = Ambros | first1 = V.
| s2cid = 13103224
 }}</ref> had revealed that a gene known as ''lin-4'' was important for normal larval development of ''C. elegans'', a nematode often studied as a model organism. Specifically, ''lin-4'' was responsible for the progressive repression of the protein [[LIN-14]] during larval development of the worm; mutant worms deficient in ''lin-4'' function had persistently high levels of LIN-14 and displayed developmental timing defects.<ref name="hierarchy" />

Ambros and colleagues found that ''lin-4'', unexpectedly, did not encode a regulatory protein. Instead, it gave rise to some small RNA molecules, 22 and 61 nucleotides in length, which Ambros called lin-4S (short) and lin-4L (long). Sequence analysis showed that lin-4S was part of lin-4L: lin-4L was predicted to form a stem-loop structure, with lin-4S contained in one of the arms, the 5' arm. Furthermore, Ambros, together with [[Gary Ruvkun]] (Harvard), discovered that lin-4S was partially complementary to several sequences in the 3' untranslated region of the messenger RNA encoding the LIN-14 protein.<ref>{{Cite journal
| pmid = 8252622
| year = 1993
| last1 = Wightman | first1 = B.
| last2 = Ha | first2 = I.
| last3 = Ruvkun | first3 = G.
| title = Posttranscriptional regulation of the heterochronic gene lin-14 by lin-4 mediates temporal pattern formation in C. Elegans
| volume = 75
| issue = 5
| pages = 855–862
| journal = Cell
| doi = 10.1016/0092-8674(93)90530-4
| doi-access = free
}}</ref> Ambros and colleagues hypothesized and later determined that ''lin-4'' could regulate LIN-14 through binding of lin-4S to these sequences in the ''lin-14'' transcript in a type of antisense RNA mechanism.<ref name="Cell" />

In 2000, another ''C. elegans'' small RNA regulatory molecule, [[Let-7 microRNA precursor|let-7]], was characterized by the Ruvkun lab <ref>{{cite journal
 | year = 2000
 | title = The 21-nucleotide let-7 RNA regulates developmental timing in Caenorhabditis elegans
 | journal = Nature
 | volume = 403
 | issue = 6772
 | pages = 901–906
 | pmid = 10706289
 | last1 = Reinhart | first1 = B. J.
 | last2 = Slack | first2 = F. J.
 | last3 = Basson | first3 = M.
 | last4 = Pasquinelli | first4 = A. E.
 | last5 = Bettinger | first5 = J. C.
 | last6 = Rougvie | first6 = A. E.
 | last7 = Horvitz | first7 = H. R.
 | last8 = Ruvkun | first8 = G.
 | doi = 10.1038/35002607
|bibcode = 2000Natur.403..901R | s2cid = 4384503
 }}</ref> and found to be conserved in many species, including vertebrates.<ref>{{cite journal
 | year = 2000
 | title = Conservation of the sequence and temporal expression of let-7 heterochronic regulatory RNA | first19 = E.
 | last19 = Ruvkun | first18 = P.
 | last18 = Davidson | first17 = M.
 | last17 = Leahy | first16 = J.
 | last16 = Levine | first15 = J.
 | last15 = Corbo | first14 = M.
 | last14 = Finnerty | first13 = A.
 | last13 = Fishman | first12 = J. R.
 | last12 = Srinivasan
 | journal = Nature | first11 = P.
 | volume = 408
 | issue = 6808
 | last11 = Spring
 | pages = 86–89
 | pmid = 11081512
 | first10 = B.
 | last1 = Pasquinelli | first1 = A. E.
 | last2 = Reinhart | first2 = B. J.
 | last3 = Slack
 | last10 = Müller | first3 = F.
 | last4 = Martindale | first4 = M. Q.
 | last5 = Kuroda | first5 = M. I.
 | last6 = Maller | first6 = B.
 | last7 = Hayward | first7 = D. C.
 | last8 = Ball | first8 = E. E.
 | last9 = Degnan | first9 = B.
 | doi = 10.1038/35040556 | bibcode = 2000Natur.408...86P
| s2cid = 4401732 }}</ref> These discoveries, among others, confirmed that Ambros had in fact discovered a class of small RNAs with conserved functions, now known as [[microRNA]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bartel |first1=David P. |title=Metazoan MicroRNAs |journal=Cell |date=March 2018 |volume=173 |issue=1 |pages=20–51 |doi=10.1016/j.cell.2018.03.006|pmid=29570994 |pmc=6091663 }}</ref>

Ambros was elected to the [[United States National Academy of Sciences]] in 2007.<ref name="NAS">{{cite web |title=Victor R. Ambros – NAS |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/victor-r-ambros-fhumzl/ |website=National Academy of Sciences |access-date=9 October 2024}}</ref> He was elected a Fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 2011.<ref name="umass">{{cite web |title=Learn more about Victor Ambros |url=https://www.umassmed.edu/news/news-archives/2024/10/learn-more-about-victor-ambros-phd/ |website=UMass Chan Medical School |access-date=9 October 2024 |language=en |date=7 October 2024 |archive-date=October 8, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241008031018/https://www.umassmed.edu/news/news-archives/2024/10/learn-more-about-victor-ambros-phd/ |url-status=live }}</ref> In 2024 he shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology and Medicine with Gary Ruvkun "for the discovery of microRNA and its role in post-transcriptional gene regulation".<ref name="NobelPrize" />
